title: Pointers: addresses and dereferencing
body: A pointer is a variable that stores the address of another object. & gives an object's address and * dereferences a pointer to reach the object it points to. A pointer's type decides how many bytes are read through it and how far p + 1 moves: one whole element, not one byte. Passing a pointer to a function lets the function change the caller's variable, because C itself always passes arguments by value. Initialise pointers before use, set them to NULL when they point nowhere, and never dereference NULL or an uninitialised pointer.
interview_tip: Be ready to explain why swap(int a, int b) cannot swap the caller's variables but swap(int *a, int *b) can.

title: Arrays vs pointers
body: In most expressions an array name decays to a pointer to its first element, so arr[i] means *(arr + i). The decay does not happen with sizeof or &: sizeof(arr) is the whole array's size. A function parameter declared as int a[] is really int *a, so sizeof inside the function gives the pointer size, not the array size; pass the length as a separate argument. Unlike a pointer variable, an array name cannot be reassigned. A string literal is a char array ending in '\0'; strlen counts characters before that terminator, while sizeof on a char array counts every byte.
interview_tip: A classic trap: computing an array's length with sizeof inside a function that received the array as a parameter.

title: Dynamic memory: malloc, calloc, realloc, free
body: Heap memory is requested at run time and lives until you free it. malloc(n) returns n uninitialised bytes; calloc(count, size) returns zero-filled memory; realloc(p, n) resizes a block and may move it, so keep the old pointer until the call succeeds. All three return NULL on failure, so check the result. free(p) releases the block. Common bugs: memory leaks (losing the last pointer to a block), dangling pointers (using memory after free or returning the address of a local variable), and double free. Setting a pointer to NULL after freeing it helps prevent accidental reuse.
interview_tip: Interviewers often ask malloc vs calloc: calloc zero-initialises the memory and takes the element count and element size as separate arguments.

title: Storage classes and variable lifetime
body: Storage class decides a variable's lifetime, scope and linkage. auto (the default for locals) lives on the stack only while its block runs and starts with an indeterminate value. static on a local variable keeps one copy for the whole program run, initialised once (to zero if not given a value), so it remembers values between calls. static on a global or function limits it to the current file. extern declares a variable defined in another file. register is only a hint and you cannot take the address of a register variable. Global and static variables are zero-initialised automatically; automatic locals are not.
interview_tip: Explain the two meanings of static: persistent lifetime for local variables, and internal (file-only) linkage for globals and functions.

title: Operators, types and conversions
body: Integer division truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3; make one operand floating point to get 3.5. % works only on integers. In mixed expressions, operands are converted to a common type, so an int compared with an unsigned int is converted to unsigned and -1 becomes a huge value. && and || short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only when needed. Bitwise &, |, ^, ~, << and >> work on individual bits. Avoid expressions such as i++ + ++i that modify a variable twice without sequencing; their behaviour is undefined, so there is no single correct output.
interview_tip: If a question shows i = i++ or i++ + ++i, say the behaviour is undefined rather than guessing a number; that answer impresses interviewers.
